intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that dystonia-25 (DYT25) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the GNAL gene (139312) on chromosome 18p11.

checks.claim: Dystonia-25 (DYT25) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the GNAL gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Since dystonia is rare and inherited in an AD manner in these pedigrees, the causative mutation is expected to be an extremely rare heterozygous variant, shared by all affected family members.
checks.explanation: Paper reports GNAL mutations causing PTD, identified as heterozygous shared variants; DYT25 designation is nomenclature.

checks.claim: The GNAL gene is located on chromosome 18p11.
checks.evidence_quote: GNAL is located on chromosome 18p centromeric to the DYT7 locus for focal dystonia
checks.explanation: Paper gives 18p; 18p11 is standard cytogenetic nomenclature.

paragraphs.text: Dystonia-25 is an autosomal dominant form of primary torsion dystonia. It usually begins in adulthood, most often as cervical dystonia. It may stay focal, but in many patients it spreads to other sites, including cranial regions, with speech involvement in some; arm involvement is less common (Fuchs et al., 2013). Fuchs et al. (2013) noted reduced penetrance for primary torsion dystonia in general.

checks.evidence_quote: Since dystonia is rare and inherited in an AD manner in these pedigrees
checks.explanation: AD inheritance in GNAL PTD families.

checks.evidence_quote: Average age of dystonia onset in the carriers was 31.3, and ranged from 7–54 years.

checks.evidence_quote: Most carriers (82%) had onset in the neck, and 93% had neck involvement at final exam

checks.evidence_quote: Further, cranial involvement was present in 57% of carriers, and 44% had speech involvement.

paragraphs.text: Fuchs et al. (2013) reported 8 multiplex families with autosomal dominant primary torsion dystonia. Affected members mostly had onset in adulthood, and neck involvement (cervical dystonia) was the most common first sign. In many patients the dystonia later spread to cranial regions, speech, or the arms. Some affected individuals had focal dystonia, and others had segmental or more widespread dystonia.

checks.evidence_quote: The phenotype in the 8 multiplex families is predominantly one of cervical dystonia
checks.explanation: 8 multiplex families; AD inheritance stated elsewhere.

checks.explanation: Mostly adult onset (Table 1 shows only a few onset <18).

paragraphs.text: Fuchs et al. (2013) performed exome sequencing in individuals from 2 families with primary torsion dystonia and found heterozygous mutations in the GNAL gene that segregated with the disorder. Sanger sequencing of the coding region of GNAL in 39 additional multiplex families with primary torsion dystonia identified further heterozygous GNAL mutations in 6 families, including missense and truncating changes. GNAL encodes the stimulatory G protein alpha subunit G-alpha-olf, which in striatal medium spiny neurons couples dopamine D1 receptors and adenosine A2A receptors to adenylyl cyclase. In functional assays, Fuchs et al. (2013) found that some of the mutations impaired the function of the protein.

checks.claim: Fuchs et al. (2013) performed exome sequencing in individuals from 2 families with primary torsion dystonia.
checks.evidence_quote: We performed exome sequencing in individuals from two families with PTD

checks.claim: Exome sequencing in 2 families with primary torsion dystonia identified heterozygous mutations in the GNAL gene.
checks.evidence_quote: the causative mutation is expected to be an extremely rare heterozygous variant, shared by all affected family members. Comparing sequenced family members, we found 11,124 heterozygous shared variants in Fam P and 4,578 in Fam D1.
checks.explanation: GNAL variants p.S293X and p.V137M were found among heterozygous shared variants.

checks.claim: The heterozygous GNAL mutations found by exome sequencing in 2 primary torsion dystonia families segregated with the disorder.
checks.evidence_quote: the p.S293X variant in the GNAL gene co-segregated with dystonia in the remaining members of Fam P
checks.explanation: p.V137M also segregated in Fam D1.

checks.claim: Fuchs et al. (2013) performed Sanger sequencing of the GNAL coding region in 39 additional multiplex families with primary torsion dystonia.
checks.evidence_quote: we performed Sanger sequencing of the entire coding region in 39 additional multiplex PTD families of mixed European origin who were mutation negative for DYT1 and DYT6.

checks.claim: Sanger sequencing of GNAL in 39 additional multiplex primary torsion dystonia families identified heterozygous GNAL mutations in 6 families.
checks.evidence_quote: We detected novel mutations in the GNAL gene in six additional families (19%)

checks.claim: The GNAL mutations identified in the additional primary torsion dystonia families included missense changes.
checks.evidence_quote: including one nonsense (p.R21X), two frameshift (p.S95fsX110 and p.R198fsX210), one missense (p.E155K)

checks.claim: The GNAL mutations identified in the additional primary torsion dystonia families included truncating changes.
checks.evidence_quote: including one nonsense (p.R21X), two frameshift (p.S95fsX110 and p.R198fsX210)

checks.claim: GNAL encodes the stimulatory G protein alpha subunit G-alpha-olf.
checks.evidence_quote: GNAL encodes the stimulatory alpha subunit, Gαolf

checks.claim: In striatal medium spiny neurons, G-alpha-olf couples dopamine D1 receptors to adenylyl cyclase.
checks.evidence_quote: In MSNs, Gαolf couples dopamine type 1 receptors (D1R) of the direct pathway and adenosine A2A receptors (A2AR) of the indirect pathway to the activation of adenylyl cyclase type 5 (AC5)

checks.claim: In striatal medium spiny neurons, G-alpha-olf couples adenosine A2A receptors to adenylyl cyclase.
checks.evidence_quote: In MSNs, Gαolf couples dopamine type 1 receptors (D1R) of the direct pathway and adenosine A2A receptors (A2AR) of the indirect pathway to the activation of adenylyl cyclase type 5 (AC5)

checks.claim: In functional assays, Fuchs et al. (2013) found that some of the dystonia-associated GNAL mutations impaired G-alpha-olf protein function.
checks.evidence_quote: Impaired function of several of the mutants was shown by bioluminescence resonance energy transfer (BRET) assays.

paragraphs.text: G-alpha-olf mediates dopamine D1 receptor and adenosine A2A receptor signaling in striatal medium spiny neurons. Fuchs et al. (2013) proposed that loss of G-alpha-olf function disrupts this striatal signaling, and that this may lead to dystonia.

checks.claim: G-alpha-olf mediates dopamine D1 receptor signaling in striatal medium spiny neurons.
checks.evidence_quote: In MSNs, Gαolf couples dopamine type 1 receptors (D1R) of the direct pathway and adenosine A2A receptors (A2AR) of the indirect pathway to the activation of adenylyl cyclase type 5 (AC5)

checks.claim: G-alpha-olf mediates adenosine A2A receptor signaling in striatal medium spiny neurons.
checks.evidence_quote: In MSNs, Gαolf couples dopamine type 1 receptors (D1R) of the direct pathway and adenosine A2A receptors (A2AR) of the indirect pathway to the activation of adenylyl cyclase type 5 (AC5)

checks.claim: Fuchs et al. (2013) proposed that loss of G-alpha-olf function disrupts striatal dopamine D1 and adenosine A2A receptor signaling.
checks.evidence_quote: Identification of causative mutations in GNAL points to primary abnormalities of D1R and/or A2AR transmission as possibly leading to dystonia.
checks.explanation: Together with the loss-of-function suggestion from the functional assay.

checks.claim: Fuchs et al. (2013) proposed that disruption of striatal signaling caused by loss of G-alpha-olf function may lead to dystonia.
checks.evidence_quote: A functional assay testing several of the mutations is suggestive of a loss of function. Along with mutations in the tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) biosynthetic pathway in dopa-responsive dystonia (DRD), GNAL directly points to the dopamine and/or adenosine signal transduction pathways as the origin of dystonia pathophysiology.
